Description
The McCracken Lab at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi seeks a highly motivated and talented PhD student to join our collaborative and dynamic research team starting Spring 2027. This position offers the opportunity to conduct cutting-edge research on the Texas tortoise (Gopherus berlandieri), a species of significant ecological and conservation importance in South Texas. This research will involve a combination of fieldwork in rugged South Texas habitats, laboratory analysis, and ecological modeling, focusing on aspects of movement ecology, habitat and resource use, and/or translocation biology of the Texas tortoise.

About the Position
Primary Responsibilities:
Conduct field-based research on tortoise movement ecology using GPS telemetry and other innovative tracking methods.
Conduct habitat-use, resource-selection, and behavioral observations to characterize Texas tortoise ecology and inform conservation management.
Develop research questions and complementary study components within the scope of ongoing projects, while ensuring the fulfillment of funding agency objectives and reporting requirements.
Perform data analyses and prepare technical reports, manuscripts, and other deliverables for grant-funded projects.
Support investigations of disease prevalence and its effects on tortoise health, survival, and population dynamics.
Evaluate translocation outcomes and develop evidence-based strategies to improve conservation effectiveness.
Collaborate with state and federal agencies, conservation organizations, and private landowners to advance Texas tortoise management and recovery efforts.
Additional Opportunities:
Mentor undergraduate researchers in the lab and field.
Present findings at regional, national, and international conferences.

Qualifications
Required Qualifications:
Master’s degree in biology, wildlife ecology, or related field.
Experience with fieldwork in adverse conditions, particularly with herpetofauna or other wildlife.
Experience in data management and strong analytical skills.
Experience working with the programming language R
Strong communication skills (written and verbal in English) and a history of collaboration in professional team settings.
Demonstrated ability to work independently while contributing effectively within interdisciplinary research teams.
Strong self-motivation, professionalism, positive attitude, and interpersonal communication skills.
Valid driver’s license.
Preferred Qualifications:
Skills in GIS, telemetry, or statistical modeling are highly desirable.
Experience working with state or federal agencies, non-profit organizations, or private stakeholders.
Experience presenting research findings at scientific conferences.
Experience preparing manuscripts for publication or grant reports.
A passion for conservation and working in challenging field conditions.

What We Offer
Fully funded research expenses.
Funding opportunities for a competitive stipend and tuition coverage.
Access to state-of-the-art facilities and equipment.
Mentorship from an engaged and interdisciplinary team of researchers.
The opportunity to work in diverse ecosystems focusing on applied conservation science.

How to Apply
Interested candidates should submit the following:
A cover letter detailing research interests, career goals, and relevant experience (up to 400 words)
Curriculum Vitae (CV).
Contact information for three academic references.
Academic transcripts (unofficial copies are acceptable initially).
Please submit the above documents as a single PDF file Tortoise-PHD-LastName_Firstname].pdf and use ‘Texas tortoise PhD position 2027’ as subject line for the email to Dr. Shawn McCracken (shawn.mccracken@tamucc.edu). Applications will be reviewed on a rolling basis, with priority given to those received by September 14, 2026. The chosen applicant must submit all application documents by October 1, 2026.
Join the McCracken Lab
TAMUCC, located in Corpus Christi, TX, offers a unique coastal setting with access to diverse ecosystems and a vibrant research community. Join us in making a meaningful impact on the conservation of this iconic species and its habitats.
For more information, please contact Dr. McCracken.
Contact
Dr. Shawn McCracken
shawn.mccracken@tamucc.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
The University of Alaska Fairbanks, College of Fisheries and Ocean Sciences (CFOS) is recruiting 8 PhD students to start in Spring, Summer or Fall 2027 through a new program called EMERGE Alaska.

EMERGE Alaska is a National Science Foundation (NSF) funded program for U.S. students who received an Honorable Mention on the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP) during the last 3 years. The Fellowship covers stipend, tuition, fees, and health insurance for 3 years.

EMERGE Alaska focuses on marine and coastal ecosystem research, and is anchored on four components: academic training, research and innovation, professional development, and student success support. EMERGE Alaska is housed in CFOS, one of the largest and most geographically diverse academic and research organizations in Alaska.

UAF CFOS has three departments (Fisheries, Marine Biology, and Oceanography) whose 42 faculty and 138 graduate students work with local communities, Tribes, agencies, and the fishing industry, and do research from the Arctic to the Antarctic, including inland waters, coastal systems, and the deep ocean. CFOS operates NSF’s R/V Sikuliaq, an ice-capable research ship, as well as smaller research vessels, and has coastal research and laboratory facilities in Juneau, Seward, and Kachemak Bay.

The next deadline to apply is September 15, 2026. Eligible applicants must be U.S. Citizens, Nationals or green card holders who have already received the honorable mention. For more information and links to apply via NSF’s ETAP portal, visit our program website.
Contact
Jessica Glass
jrglass@alaska.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
 I want to bring to your attention to an open graduate student position in the Schweikert Lab at the Department of Biology and Marine Biology at the University of North Carolina Wilmington (UNCW).  Applicants with experience in neurophysiological or behavioral approaches are preferred, though not required. 

 PhD in Integrative, Comparative, and Marine Biology: Neuroethology of Adaptive Camouflage in Flatfishes (starting Fall 2027) 

Prior to applying to the UNCW graduate program, interested students should email Dr. Lorian Schweikert (schweikertl@uncw.edu) with the following: 
·      Statement of career goals and research interests (1 page max) 
·      Resume or CV 
·      Unofficial transcripts 
·      Contact information for three references 
 Priority deadline for contacting Dr. Schweikert about the PhD position is September 13th, 2026. Interviews will begin in fall, though interest emails will be accepted until the position is filled. The UNCW application deadline for the PhD position is February 15th, 2027. 
 Program Synopsis: 
Dynamic color change allows animals such as certain marine fishes to rapidly change the color and pattern of their skin, yet knowledge is lacking about how these animals gather and process the visual information needed to make color change decisions. Recent discoveries suggest that many color-changing animals can detect light with their skin, a process known as dermal photoreception, which may work alongside the eyes to regulate color change. Our lab investigates how dermal photoreception contributes to color change in fishes and whether the skin acts as a sensory system for monitoring the environment or the animal’s own coloration. By uncovering the principles underlying distributed light sensing and adaptive camouflage, the project may inform future technologies related to bioinspired sensing and material science. 
 Additional Resources: 
For more information on the Schweikert Lab, please visit: https://www.schweikertlab.com/ 
 For more information on the Biology/Marine Biology Department at UNCW, visit: https://uncw.edu/bio/ 
 For more information on UNCWs Center for Marine Science, please visit: https://uncw.edu/cms/ 
  Contact
Lorian Schweikert

 Position Title: M.S. or Ph.D. Graduate Assistantship: Strategies and technologies to enhance habitat restoration of degraded rangelands

Position Description: We are seeking a highly motivated M.S. or Ph.D. student to work on an exciting project at the intersection of restoration ecology, geospatial data science and ecological modelling. The graduate student selected will conduct research on habitat restoration of degraded rangelands (e.g., energy extraction, woody plant encroachment, and rangeland conversion). Project goals include using native species restoration, prescribed fire, and adaptive grazing to reduce the risks and impacts of drought and invasive plant species, as well as to address issues related to woody encroachment to enhance wildlife habitat in Texas. The successful candidate will pursue an M.S. or Ph.D. (depending on qualifications) degree in Range and Wildlife Management (M.S.) or Wildlife and Rangeland Sciences (Ph.D.) with the Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute, Department of Rangeland and Wildlife Sciences, Texas A&M University-Kingsville. Additional duties include publication of research results; presentations at professional conferences; assisting with other projects and other duties as assigned.

Required Qualifications:
·       B.S. (for M.S. position) or M.S. (for Ph.D.) in rangeland science, plant ecology, botany, environmental science, geography or closely related field. 
·       Excellent written and verbal communication skills in English.
·       Strong quantitative and problem-solving skills.
·       Strong work ethic, ability to work independently and as a productive member of a research team.
·       Ability to work under adverse field conditions (hot humid environment). 
 Preferred Qualifications: 
·       Background in plant identification, and experience basic field ecology and surveying vegetation.
·       Experience with geospatial technologies such as GPS and Geographic Information Systems (GIS).
·       Familiarity with geospatial data (climate, vegetation, soil), remote sensing data products.
·       A strong interest in ecological modeling and data science.
·       Ability and willingness to drive vehicle and lead field survey in difficult terrain/weather.
 Stipend/Salary: $2,000/month for M.S., $2,500/month for Ph.D., plus benefits (medical package available after completion of waiting period). Nonresident tuition is waived (resident tuition and fees apply). Partial resident tuition fee assistance may be provided based on availability of funds.

Description
 We are seeking a highly motivated M.Sc. student to conduct experimental research examining the cascading ecological consequences of rodent population cycles. The student will work with Dr. Robert McCleery (University of Florida) and Dr. Mike Conner (Jones Center at Ichauway), with all field research conducted at the Jones Center at Ichauway in southwestern Georgia. 

The project 
Rodent populations can undergo dramatic changes in abundance over relatively short periods, yet we still have a limited understanding of how these fluctuations propagate through ecological communities. This project will use a large-scale manipulative field experiment with cotton rats to determine how major shifts in rodent abundance influence other components of the ecosystem. 

The student will experimentally manipulate cotton rat populations and quantify responses across multiple trophic levels, including: 
predators
Birds and other prey species
vegetation
insect communities
The project provides an opportunity to conduct rigorous experimental field ecology while addressing fundamental questions about population dynamics, species interactions, and trophic cascades. The student will be closely involved in designing and implementing experiments, collecting and managing field data, analyzing results, and communicating findings through scientific presentations and publications.
 We are looking for a student who has 

A strong interest in population, community, and experimental ecology.
Meaningful field research experience, with experience handling or trapping rodents or other small mammals particularly desirable.
Strong problem-solving skills and the ability to adapt when field research does not go according to plan.
The ability to work both independently and collaboratively as part of a research team.
Strong organizational and data-management skills.
Good scientific writing and communication skills.
A strong work ethic and enthusiasm for intensive field-based research.

This position is particularly well suited for someone who wants to develop as an independent field ecologist and gain experience conducting a manipulative ecological experiment from field implementation through analysis and publication.
 
Support
The position is funded for two years and includes a graduate stipend, tuition support, and project-related field and research expenses.

To apply
Interested applicants should send [application materials — e.g., CV, brief statement of research interests and experience, unofficial transcripts, and contact information for three references] to [ramccleery@ufl.edu and Mike.Conner@jonesctr.org].

In your statement, please describe your previous field research experience, particularly any experience working with small mammals, and provide examples of situations in which you have had to solve problems independently while conducting research.

Review of applications will begin 9/11 and continue until the position is filled.
 
  Contact
Robert McCleery
352-846-0566
ramccleery@ufl.edu (preferred contact method)

Description
A two-year postdoctoral fellowship is available with Dr. Mitch Weegman in the Department of Biology at the University of Saskatchewan (https://www.ducks.ca/our-work/science/saskatchewan-endowed-chair/), in collaboration with Drs. Todd Arnold (Delta Waterfowl Foundation) and Matt Dyson (Ducks Unlimited Canada). The postdoctoral fellow will lead a research project estimating the population dynamics of North American ducks and their environmental drivers, using 65-year data sets to address long-standing questions about synchrony in multispecies demographic rates as well as the impact of agricultural intensity (e.g., pesticide application rates in the Canadian prairies) and cross-seasonal effects on duck reproductive success, survival, and population structure. This work extends substantial ecological and statistical developments on duck population dynamics led by the late Dr. Dan Gibson (University of Minnesota/University of Saskatchewan).
 Our team has focused on estimating the effects of habitat and harvest management on demographic rates in northern pintails, using an integrated metapopulation model to link pintail demography within and among breeding and wintering regions. We anticipate expanding this model to multiple dabbling and diving duck species for greater ecological perspective and conservation utility. We also anticipate exploring linkages between demographic rates and pesticide, insecticide and fungicide application rates across the Canadian prairies, for fuller context about relationships between agricultural intensification and duck reproductive success. There will be opportunities to explore related research questions and collaborate on several projects in movement and population ecology in the Weegman lab, as well as with Delta Waterfowl Foundation and Ducks Unlimited Canada.
 Prerequisites: Ideal candidates will have a PhD in ecology, statistics or a closely related field, and interpersonal skills to lead discussions among collaborators. Preference will be given to those with a strong quantitative background (e.g., experience with Program R, Bayesian methods) and knowledge of migratory bird ecology and management. Students must have a valid driver’s license. The successful applicant will be expected to publish manuscripts in peer-reviewed journals and present papers at scientific meetings.
 Salary and benefits: $65,000 Canadian per year plus benefits
 Start date: 1 January or 1 September 2027

Description
Dr. Lisa Izzo (Fisheries and Aquatic Conservation Ecology Lab) in the School of Natural Resources at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville is seeking applicants for a M.S. student in Wildlife and Fisheries Science. The student’s thesis work will focus on understanding movements of adult lake sturgeon in the Tennessee River using acoustic telemetry, with a particular emphasis on locating potential spawning areas and documenting successful spawning via egg and/or larval drift sampling. This collaborative project will give the student the opportunity to work closely with project partners including the Tennessee Wildlife Resources Agency (TWRA), Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), and others. 
 Duties: In addition to course requirements of the M.S. in Wildlife and Fisheries Science program, primary duties of the student will include (1) surgical tagging and active tracking of adult lake sturgeon; (2) maintenance of a stationary acoustic receiver array; (3) study design and deployment of various gears to sample sturgeon eggs and larvae; (4) data management and analysis; (5) presentations to project partners and at regional/national conferences; and (6) writing of a final thesis, at least one manuscript for submission to a peer-reviewed journal, and reports to project funders. The selected applicant will have the opportunity to develop and investigate hypotheses and address objectives of interest within the context of the project. Field work will take place at large river/reservoir sites, so trailering, launching, driving, and working on boats is required. Field work may take place at irregular hours, especially larval sampling.   
 Location: The position will be based at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. 
 Start Date: November 1, 2026 preferred, January 2027 at the latest (Contingent on funding timeline) 
 Qualifications: Successful applicants must have a Bachelor’s degree in Natural Resources, Ecology, Wildlife Science/Management, Fisheries Science/Management, or a closely related field, and meet all other qualifications for admission to the School of Natural Resources Master’s Program (https://naturalresources.tennessee.edu/masters-program/). Please note that GRE scores are optional for admission. Applicants should have an interest in aquatic research and fisheries management, and a strong desire to learn new skills through the graduate school process. The successful candidate must possess a valid driver’s license and be able to lead field work independently. Prior experience in aquatic field work (particularly on boats), minor boat maintenance, acoustic telemetry equipment, and/or data analysis and management in statistical software is preferred but not required. 
 Salary and Benefits: $37,000/year stipend for 3 years, coverage for tuition, and health insurance benefits. The student will be responsible for paying graduate student fees. 
 To Apply: Please email (1) a one-page statement of research interests and career goals, (2) a CV, (3) unofficial transcripts, and (4) contact information for three references to Dr. Lisa Izzo (lizzo1@utk.edu) with a subject line of MS Application Lake Sturgeon and your last name. Applications are due September 7th and review will begin immediately after. Successful candidate will apply formally to the UTK graduate school following the internal application process.
Contact
Lisa Izzo
lizzo1@utk.edu (preferred contact method)

Postdoc Summary:
The Wildlife and Water Lab (WWL), based at the Odum School of
Ecology, University of Georgia (UGA), Athens, invites applications for a postdoctoral
candidate in Spatial Biodiversity Data and Conservation Applications beginning January 15,
2027 (or earlier if possible). The position is 2-year (24 months) non-tenure track
appointment, and the salary is competitive and commensurate with qualifications and
experience. The successful candidate will conduct quantitative analyses of the
ecohydrology of terrestrial birds and participate in an ongoing, multi-institution project
developing frameworks and support tools for measuring the biodiversity enhancement
(i.e., net gain) of projects under the IUCN Global Standard for Nature-based Solutions’
Criterion 3.

Responsibilities: 
The postdoctoral associate will work under the mentorship of Dr.
Charles van Rees (Odum School of Ecology) and in collaboration with graduate students
in the WWL and other faculty at UGA on (1) spatial ecological research on the
relationship between terrestrial birds, wetlands, and riparian habitats, and (2)
biodiversity accounting for Nature-based Solutions projects. Specific responsibilities
include (a) accessing, processing, managing, and analyzing large datasets including
river flow data, remote sensing imagery, and spatially explicit biodiversity data (e.g.,
eBird, NEON), (b) testing ecological hypotheses through quantitative spatial analysis,
including via machine learning and Bayesian approaches, (c) developing browser-based
decision-making tools from existing frameworks and publicly available datasets, and (d)
leveraging and training Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents to support decision-making tool
functionality. The successful candidate will interface with collaborators at partner
institutions, lead group meetings, and mentor one or more graduate students in each
project capacity. The postdoc will present the project results at national conferences and
will engage with other career development opportunities on and off campus, such as
teaching and other professional development (grant management, etc.) workshops
whenever suitable.


Required qualifications: 
In addition to a PhD degree in Ecology, Biology, or other
related fields and a strong publication record, competitive candidates must have proven
abilities to conduct statistical analyses using publicly available large datasets and to
work as part of a scientific team. Especially competitive candidates will have familiarity
either with the concepts of Nature-based Solutions, biodiversity accounting or net-gain,
and the IUCN Global Standard or with the ecology of riparian birds, emergent aquatic
insects, or river systems. Experience and proficiency in Python and/or Javascript is
required, and experience working with and developing AI-enabled decision-making
tools is welcome and encouraged. Strong written and verbal communication skills are
required.

The candidate will be based in the Water and Wildlife Lab (https://vanreeslab.ecology.uga.edu/) in the Odum School of
Ecology at the University of Georgia, and will also be an affiliate of the Institute for
Resilient Infrastructure Systems (IRIS; https://iris.uga.edu/) at UGA.


The position will include retirement and health benefits. Interested candidates should
apply online through UGA Jobs at https://www.ugajobsearch.com/postings/501516. Any
questions about the position should be directed to Dr. Charles van Rees
(Charles.vanrees@uga.edu). Review of applications will begin immediately and continue
until the position is filled. The University of Georgia values diversity, and all qualified
applicants are encouraged to apply. UGA is in Athens, GA, a vibrant mid-sized city
renowned for its music scene, restaurants, and cultural opportunities.

Description
 Azura is seeking a Diadromous Fisheries Analyst to support the NOAA Fisheries Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) Protected Species Division (PSD). 
 The Gulf of Maine Distinct Population Segment (GOM DPS) of Atlantic salmon is listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act and remains a NOAA ‘Species in the Spotlight’. Although individual factors like dams and marine survival have been identified as priorities for salmon recovery, identifying the appropriate combination of existing and potentially new specific management actions that considers the present and future threat of climate change remains challenging. To overcome this, the Northeast Atlantic Salmon Team is following a 5-step approach to advance climate mitigation ideas into tangible climate actions to recover the species. This 5-step approach consists of: 1) developing National Climate Science Strategy/Regional Action Plans, 2) performing Climate Vulnerability Assessments, 3) conducting Scenario Planning, 4) conducting identified science and modeling efforts, and 5) developing climate-ready conservation and management actions. NEFSC has completed steps 1 through 3. The successful applicant will help advance steps 4 and 5. When complete, this effort will identify the appropriate combination of existing and new management actions that consider current and projected future climate impacts, which have the highest probability of achieving the recovery criteria outlined within the final recovery plan of the GOM DPS. 
 This position is part of a larger project, which will culminate with the completion of a number of Management Strategy Evaluations (MSEs) on the management interventions identified to assess their likelihood to mitigate the impacts of the stressors identified and to contribute to the recovery of the GOM DPS. The successful candidate for this position will work closely with other collaborators on this project, while possibly contributing to these additional products. 
 Having high attention to detail and the ability to manage short project timelines are critical skills for this position. Potential candidates must also possess the ability to manage a project to its completion, resulting in a peer-reviewed manuscript and identify and mine scientific publications for relevant information. Applicants must be able to operate independently, manage their own work schedule, and dedicate blocks of time for uninterrupted focus, while effectively working and communicating with collaborators to meet project objectives. 
 Place of Performance and Work Schedule 
The preferred place of performance is the Woods Hole, Massachusetts area or the Greater Orono or Bangor, Maine area. A remote location within the U.S. may be considered as an alternate place of performance. During workdays, candidates must be able to respond to all communications within 24 hours and conduct calls and meetings as necessary during normal business hours. Work is full-time (40 hours per week, Monday through Friday) and expected to last approximately three years, with the possibility of extension. The estimated start date is October 1, 2026 (pending security investigation). Travel is anticipated to occur at least three times per year. This position is not open to visa sponsorship or relocation assistance. 
 Compensation and Benefits 
Rate: $35.34/hour 
Competitive benefits include medical, dental, and vision insurance; 401k with employer match; life and disability insurance; and paid time off for vacation, sick leave, and company-observed holidays. 
 Duties 
The employee will work collaboratively with an Oversight Committee consisting of representatives from NOAA’s NEFSC and Greater Atlantic Regional Fisheries Office and others, as appropriate, to advance progress under the two linked objectives described below. 
Under Objective 1, the employee will: 
review existing syntheses pertinent to the recovery of the GOM DPS of Atlantic salmon such as the Final Recovery Plan, the Atlantic Salmon Scenario Planning exercise, the Climate Vulnerability Analysis, and related peer-reviewed and gray literature and communicate with relevant experts; 
develop a semi-quantitative classification model to rank the impact of anthropogenic factors (i.e., “stressors”), considering the present and future threat of climate change, on the productivity of the GOM DPS of Atlantic salmon, similar to that produced for Norwegian Atlantic salmon stocks (https://doi.org/10.1093/icesjms/fsx020); and 
lead the development of a peer-reviewed publication summarizing the outcomes of Objective 1. 
Under Objective 2, the employee will: 
review peer-reviewed and gray literature and communicate with relevant experts to identify and inventory the potential management interventions available to address each stressor identified under Objective 1;
summarize available empirical evidence of the effectiveness of each identified management intervention with a view to highlighting those options that may increase smolt output, in light of the challenging conditions faced by salmon in the marine environment; and 
lead the development of a peer-reviewed publication summarizing the outcomes of Objective 2. 
Facilitate monthly meetings with the Oversight Committee (group members will provide expertise and guidance on identifying stressors to Atlantic salmon and available management interventions). 
 Required Qualifications 
Master’s or Doctorate degree in biological sciences, natural resource management, fisheries, quantitative ecology, or a related field
Familiarity with Atlantic salmon
Process-oriented and attentive to detail
Excellent reading comprehension and writing skills
Ability to multitask and work with short deadlines
Strong skills with MS Office, Google Suite applications, and statistical packages (i.e., R)
Eligibility to work in the U.S.
Candidate must be able to obtain a Public Trust Clearance which requires passing a thorough background check.

Azura is seeking a Diadromous Fisheries Analyst to support the NOAA Fisheries Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) Protected Species Division (PSD). 
 The Atlantic salmon population in the Gulf of Maine (GOM) is protected as endangered under the Endangered Species Act and is a top conservation priority for NOAA, requiring specialized assistance to implement critical plans and actions. This contract position will assist with implementation of four primary objectives: 1) developing, implementing, and evaluating a new Atlantic salmon marking and monitoring program on the Penobscot River; 2) assisting with activities related to a parentage analysis study using archived tissue samples to understand genetic contributions of wild versus hatchery origin individuals to annual adult returns; 3) analyzing archived smolt telemetry data to describe migration dynamics and support management thought the development of publication(s); and 4) provide general support for field activities, boat operations, maintenance, and meeting facilitation. The employee will work with the NEFSC and others, as appropriate, to advance progress under these objectives.
 Having high attention to detail and the ability to manage short project timelines are critical skills for this position. Potential candidates must also possess the ability to manage a project to its completion, resulting in a peer-reviewed manuscript, and identify and mine scientific publications for relevant information. Applicants must be able to operate independently, manage their own work schedule, and dedicate blocks of time for uninterrupted focus, while effectively working and communicating with collaborators to meet project objectives.
 Place of Performance and Work Schedule 
The place of performance is the Greater Orono or Bangor, Maine area. Work is full-time (40 hours per week, Monday through Friday) and expected to last approximately three years, with the possibility of extension. The estimated start date is October 1, 2026 (pending security investigation). Travel is anticipated to occur at least three times per year. This position is not open to visa sponsorship, relocation assistance, or remote work. 
 Compensation and Benefits 
Rate: $35.34/hour 
Competitive benefits include medical, dental, and vision insurance; 401k with employer match; life and disability insurance; and paid time off for vacation, sick leave, and company-observed holidays. 
 Duties 
The employee will perform a variety of tasks to support this project.  
Under Objective 1, the employee will:
work with identified collaborators to evaluate the current monitoring of stocking and adult returns on the Penobscot River while identifying key benefits limitations and current and future monitoring needs;
based on the previous assessment, propose and analyze alternative monitoring methods, including detailed resource requirements and a pros/cons analysis for each;
work with identified collaborators to facilitate discussions regarding feasibility, strategic alignment, and resource needs for proposed alternative methods;
synthesize collaborator feedback and prepare detailed work plans, budgets, and operational considerations for the implementation of the preferred adoption(s); and 
work with identified collaborators to implement the preferred monitoring method.
Under Objective 2, the employee will:
inventory, organize, and catalog agency and partner tissue samples archives;
generate a working summary database/spreadsheet to continue future inventory of samples collected; and 
provide support for transport of these samples for shipment to collaborators for analysis.
Under Objective 3, the employee will: 
investigate archived agency telemetry datasets to understand data structure, metadata, and study objectives;
identify datasets that have the potential to inform current management challenges and questions;  
use statistical packages to analyze selected datasets (e.g., estimate survival, migration dynamics); and
lead the development of peer-reviewed publication(s).
Under Objective 4, the employee will: 
assist with day-to-day field activities;  
participate in training required to be a NOAA small boat operator;
assist with NOAA small boat maintenance;
work with identified collaborators to initiate and further Atlantic salmon projects as directed; and 
participate in and/or lead meetings. 
 Required Qualifications 
Master’s or Doctorate degree in biological sciences, natural resource management, fisheries, quantitative ecology, or a related field
Familiarity with Atlantic salmon 
Process-oriented and attentive to detail
Excellent reading comprehension and writing skills
Ability to multitask and work with short deadlines
Strong skills with MS Office, Google Suite applications, and statistical packages (i.e., R)
Eligibility to work in the U.S.
Candidate must be able to obtain a Public Trust Clearance which requires passing a thorough background check.
